query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a very low concentration (<1 at%) of zirconium to eutectic high-entropy alloys will improve both room-temperature tensile strength and ductility by promoting Zr segregation at the internal lamellar interfaces, thereby enhancing interfacial cohesion and mitigating microcrack nucleation and propagation.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy exhibiting dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries that serve as sites for microcrack initiation during room-temperature tensile deformation.
generation.intervention: Microalloying with a dilute (<1 at%) concentration of zirconium.
generation.conditions: Samples are processed via identical casting and heat-treatment conditions designed to enable elemental segregation, and mechanical tests are conducted under room-temperature tensile deformation.
generation.structural_mediator: Zr atoms segregated to the lamellar colony interfaces.
generation.mechanism: The Zr segregation enhances the cohesion of the internal interfaces, reducing local stress concentrations and thereby impeding the initiation and propagation of microcracks. Concurrently, the strengthened interfaces can act as effective barriers to dislocation motion, leading to an improvement in both tensile strength and ductility compared to the unmodified baseline.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the unmodified alloy, the Zr-modified alloy is expected to exhibit statistically significant improvements in tensile strength and ductility, marked by a reduction in microcrack formation and an overall enhancement of mechanical performance under room-temperature tensile loading.
generation.baseline: Unmodified eutectic high-entropy alloy with dual-phase lamellar architecture, which suffers from early microcrack initiation due to weak interfacial bonding.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are contingent on maintaining the Zr concentration below 1 at% and on processing conditions that promote effective interfacial segregation. Excessive Zr or deviations in heat-treatment may result in secondary phase formation or disruption of the eutectic lamellar structure, nullifying the desired improvements.
generation.uncertainty: While the qualitative improvements in tensile strength and ductility are anticipated, the precise quantitative enhancement remains uncertain and may depend on subtle processing variations and specific alloy chemistries.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of eutectic high-entropy alloy samples from the same composition: one set with <1 at% Zr addition and a baseline set without Zr. Subject both sets to identical casting and heat-treatment protocols optimized for elemental segregation. Use high-resolution characterization techniques such as transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and atom probe tomography (APT) to assess the presence and distribution of Zr at the lamellar interfaces. Conduct standardized room-temperature tensile tests to obtain quantitative measurements of tensile strength, ductility, and microcrack formation.
measurements: Tensile strength (yield and ultimate tensile strength)
Onset load and density of microcracks via microscopic analysis
Quantitative assessment of Zr segregation at interlamellar interfaces using TEM/APT
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Zr-modified samples do not show statistically significant increases in both tensile strength and ductility compared to the baseline, or if high-resolution characterization fails to demonstrate appreciable Zr segregation at the lamellar interfaces, the hypothesis is considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract High-performance refractory alloys with ultrahigh strength and ductility are in demand for a wide range of critical applications, such as plasma-facing components. However, it remains challenging to increase the strength of these alloys without seriously compromising their tensile ductility. Here, we put forward a strategy to “defeat” this trade-off in tungsten refractory high-entropy alloys by stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitations (SCCPs). The coherent interfaces of SCCPs facilitate the dislocation transmission and relieve the stress concentrations that can lead to premature crack initiation. As a consequence, our alloy displays an ultrahigh strength of 2.15 GPa with a tensile ductility of 15% at ambient temperature, with a high yield strength of 1.05 GPa at 800 °C. The SCCPs design concept may afford a means to develop a wide range of ultrahigh-strength metallic materials by providing a pathway for alloy design. frame.understanding: Hypothesis: A single intervention by microalloying—specifically adding a low concentration (e.g., <1 at%) of an element such as zirconium (Zr) that segregates to the lamellar colony interfaces—will enhance interfacial cohesion. The enhanced interfacial bonding reduces stress concentration and impedes the nucleation and propagation of microcracks. Mechanistically, the interfacial segregation is expected to both obstruct crack initiation and provide additional barriers to dislocation motion, thereby improving strength concurrent with ductility relative to the unmodified alloy. The boundary conditions include maintaining the eutectic structure and ensuring that the microalloying element remains within a solubility limit where it localizes primarily at the interfaces. Prior evidence from grain boundary segregation in conventional alloys and similar microalloying strategies in high-performance materials supports the potential of interface engineering to mitigate brittleness. An experiment that would falsify the hypothesis involves preparing two sets of samples (with and without Zr addition), subjecting them to identical heat treatment to induce segregation, and then comparing their room-temperature tensile properties and microstructural details (via high-resolution microscopy and interfacial characterization). If the Zr-modified alloy does not demonstrate both a statistically significant increase in tensile strength and ductility or if interfacial analysis shows no appreciable segregation or cohesion enhancement relative to the baseline, the hypothesis would be falsified.

decision.trend: Early work on eutectic high‐entropy alloys (e.g., PMC4145285) demonstrated that casting routes leading to fine dual‐phase lamellar (fcc/B2) microstructures can produce high strength at room temperature but remain limited by brittle failure initiated at the many internal, interlamellar boundaries. Subsequent studies have explored a variety of processing modifications and microstructural design strategies—including thermo‐mechanical treatments and adjustments in processing parameters—to improve strength or ductility. However, these efforts have generally resulted in a trade‐off; while strength can be increased (often via cold working or heat treatment), the issue of localized stress concentration along the lamellar interfaces has persisted, leaving the brittle failure mode unresolved.
decision.unsolved: The key challenge is to strengthen the internal interfaces of the dual‐phase lamellar colonies in such a way that microcrack initiation is suppressed, allowing the alloy to simultaneously attain higher tensile strength and improved ductility at room temperature. Existing strategies have not successfully enhanced interfacial cohesion without adversely affecting the eutectic architecture.
decision.lever: targeted microalloying with a very low concentration (<1 at%) of zirconium to induce segregation at the lamellar interfaces
decision.why: Elemental segregation at internal boundaries has been shown in related alloy systems to enhance interfacial bonding and reduce stress concentration, thereby impeding microcrack initiation. This intervention directly targets the weak link of the lamellar structure and, following the trend in the literature of addressing interfacial cohesion rather than bulk composition or processing routes, offers a plausible, testable strategy to simultaneously improve room-temperature tensile strength and ductility. An experiment comparing samples with and without Zr addition under identical heat-treatment conditions—with subsequent high-resolution interfacial characterization and room-temperature tensile testing—would directly falsify the hypothesis if no improvement is observed.
